doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Conservatory study and learning to write and sight-read
summary: He studied European harmony at the conservatory, found jazz not taught, and in New York learned scoring as another source of income.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: This is the brass over here and the reeds over here. And then you learn how to score. You put all this stuff in the score, that’s a whole different thing. I went to the Conservatory before I moved to New York. I was like 18 years old and I went to the Conservatory and I learned keyboard harmony and solfeggio and all that you know. And I learned how to write European music you know. Stravinsky or let’s say Beethoven or Mozart. I learned how to put it together. So now as I said, well how can I learn Duke Ellington and Count Basie or Oliver Nelson? They say, “Well we don’t teach that here.” This was in the 50s

see? Jazz wasn’t even considered music in a lot of camps you know. It was like rap music today, you know it was like, oh wow, that’s a whole different world, you know, ether. So I say, “Well that’s my interest.” So I went to New York and I learned from other musicians I was working with, Duke Ellington, working with Count Basie, and big bands. Ray Charles. And they was writing. They was writing for different groups and whatnot. Because like if you go to New York, at that particular time, you could actually — if you could solo that was good, but you had to be able to read, you had to be able to see. You had to sight read.

And you had to be adaptable, you had to adapt a feeling. And you had to be able to solo. But if you could write arrangements that would give you another source of income you know, so you’ve got to learn how to score and write charts for a singer. You start out with a singer, you know. Actually you start out with a six piece to a five piece horn section with rhythm, and you start learning how to orchestrate stuff and treating the brass one way and treating the reeds another way, and making music, and you start writing, getting jobs writing for singers and then occasionally you’d get big band work and whatnot. So it was really, all this was really supporting yourself as a musician. You had to do all these — I call them like “lifejackets.” If you could play — because a lot of bands just wanted a soloist you know. Because guys couldn’t read so much but he can solo.
